name: Aloesin
lead: Aloesin is a chromone glucoside isolated from the Aloe plant that people use, in topical cosmetic products, to even out skin tone and fade dark spots. It works by inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin synthesis, so less pigment is produced in the treated area [4]. It is among the best-studied active constituents of Aloe vera, alongside aloe-emodin, aloin, emodin and acemannan [1].

Laboratory studies reported that aloesin competitively inhibits tyrosinase and reduces melanin production in cultured cells [4]. A 2002 controlled study in human volunteers reported that aloesin reduced the darkening that follows UV exposure on the forearm, and that it worked better in combination with arbutin than either did alone [8][11]. Reviews of botanical skin-lightening agents list aloesin among plant-derived ingredients such as arbutin, licorice extract and niacinamide that inhibit melanogenesis without killing melanocytes [2][12].

Because it is a plant-derived molecule rather than a prescription depigmenting drug, aloesin is sold as a cosmetic ingredient. Published work on isolated aloesin in people is limited to small studies; clinical trials of Aloe have mostly used whole Aloe vera preparations rather than isolated constituents [1].

paras: Aloesin is used in topical lightening and evening-tone products aimed at sun spots, age spots and uneven pigmentation. Reviews of botanical depigmenting agents place it with arbutin, gentisic acid, flavonoids, hesperidin, licorice and niacinamide as plant-derived ingredients that act on melanogenesis [2]. The same literature notes that conventional depigmenting agents such as hydroquinone, corticosteroids and kojic acid can be highly effective but raise safety concerns with long-term exposure, which is part of the interest in botanical alternatives [2].

A 2019 review of natural depigmenting and anti-aging molecules lists aloesin among the compounds reported to affect melanin synthesis, next to arbutin, kojic acid, azelaic acid, vitamin C and niacinamide [12]. A 2016 review of melanogenesis inhibitors likewise names aloesin among agents already used in topical drugs or cosmetic formulations, while noting that such compounds are characterized by limited effectiveness and adverse effects and that new ones are still being sought [6].

Outside cosmetics, aloesin has been investigated for wound healing, inflammation and metabolic effects. A 2015 review proposed aloesin, alone or blended with Aloe polysaccharides in a composition called Loesyn, as a possible medical food ingredient for oxidative stress in diabetes [9].

A 2002 paper described aloesin as 2-acetonyl-8-beta-D-glucopyranosyl-7-hydroxy-5-methylchromone and reported that it modulates melanogenesis by competitive inhibition of tyrosinase, acting on purified enzyme and on melanin production in vitro; kinetic studies used mushroom, human melanocyte lysate and other tyrosinase sources [4]. Tyrosinase catalyses the first steps in turning tyrosine into melanin, so blocking it lowers pigment output.

A 1999 study reported that aloesin and arbutin inhibit tyrosinase in a synergistic manner through different mechanisms [10]. Earlier work had already shown that Aloe extract inhibits mushroom tyrosinase [13]. Reviews describe aloesin as inhibiting melanogenesis without melanocyte toxicity, in contrast to agents that damage pigment cells [2].

Aloesin derivatives, including isorabaichromone, feruloylaloesin and p-coumaroylaloesin, showed antioxidant and radical-scavenging activity in laboratory assays [3]. In animal and cell work, aloesin has been reported to accelerate wound healing through MAPK/Rho and Smad signalling [7], and dietary aloesin was examined in a rat colitis model [5]. More recent animal and materials-science papers describe aloesin in a skin-regeneration scaffold, in a mouse psoriasis model and in a rat model of obesity-related liver oxidative stress [14][15][16]. These studies concern other conditions rather than cosmetic pigmentation.

The main human data on aloesin and pigmentation is a 2002 controlled study by Choi and colleagues. Volunteers had a 210 mJ dose of UV radiation delivered to the inner forearm, and the irradiated areas were assigned to a vehicle control, aloesin, arbutin, or aloesin plus arbutin [8][11]. According to the published summary, treatments were applied four times daily for 15 days; compared with control, pigmentation was reduced by 34% with aloesin, 43.5% with arbutin and 63.3% with the combination, and the aloesin effect increased with concentration [11].

This was an experimentally induced tan on forearm skin rather than a trial in people with melasma or age spots, and no larger randomized trial of isolated aloesin for existing hyperpigmentation has been identified. A 2020 review noted that clinical trials in the Aloe literature have been conducted with Aloe vera itself rather than isolated compounds and called for trials of individual metabolites [1]. A separate controlled trial of Aloe vera supplementation in prediabetes concerned blood glucose rather than skin [17].

card.summary: An Aloe-derived tyrosinase inhibitor with lab-level evidence for lightening and no published trials found.
card.note: Evidence is enzyme, cell and UV-induced pigmentation work; no controlled trials found.

quick.overview:
Aloesin is a compound from the Aloe plant studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots.
Research is mostly in test tubes, cells and a 2002 report on UV-induced pigmentation; controlled trials in people were not found.
quick.mechanism: It competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to act synergistically with arbutin.
quick.risks: No human safety data specific to topical aloesin have been reported; most reports concern laboratory and animal models.

chain: Less melanin made in treated skin
Dark spots and UV-induced tanning look lighter and more even
angle.text: Aloesin is applied to the skin as a cosmetic lightening ingredient. By slowing melanin production it is used to soften the look of sun spots and post-UV darkening, often alongside arbutin, which has a different mechanism [10].
